title: Use coordinates or extra lines to make a proof visible
chapter: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
goal: Add one helpful line, or use a grid, to make a hidden relationship visible.

scenes.visual: Two parallel lines with a bent path between them. Nothing links the bend to either line until a third parallel line fades in through the bend.
scenes.narration: Sometimes a diagram does not contain the line you need. You are allowed to add one. A good extra line connects what you know to what you want. A bad one just adds clutter, so add a line only when you can say what it is for.

scenes.visual: A cluttered diagram with many random lines beside a clean one with a single added line.
scenes.narration: Many geometry problems are one well-chosen line away from being easy. Learning which lines tend to help is a real skill: a parallel line, a height, or a line that makes a triangle with equal sides.

scenes.visual: Two horizontal parallel lines. A zigzag: from a point on the top line a segment goes down to a bend, then on to the bottom line. The angle between the top line and the first segment is 35 degrees; between the bottom line and the second segment, 45 degrees. The angle at the bend has a question mark.
scenes.narration: A path goes from one of two parallel lines to a bend, and then to the other line. It makes thirty-five degrees with the top line and forty-five degrees with the bottom line. What is the angle at the bend? Pause and think about what line you could add.

scenes.visual: A dashed line appears through the bend, parallel to both lines. It splits the bend angle into an upper and a lower part.
scenes.narration: Draw a line through the bend, parallel to the other two. It splits the bend angle into two parts.

scenes.visual: The 35 degree angle slides along the first segment to become the upper part: alternate angles. The 45 slides to become the lower part. Sum 80.
scenes.narration: The upper part matches the thirty-five degree angle, because of the parallel lines. The lower part matches the forty-five. So the angle at the bend is thirty-five plus forty-five: eighty degrees.

scenes.visual: A square grid. A tilted square has corners at grid points, each side going 3 across and 1 up. A surrounding 4 by 4 square is drawn, with four right triangles in the corners.
scenes.narration: A grid is another way to make things visible. Here is a tilted square whose sides each go three across and one up. What is its area? Surround it with a four by four square, area sixteen. The four corner triangles each have area one and a half, six altogether. Sixteen minus six is ten. The tilted square has area ten.

scenes.visual: A triangle with a height dropped from the top to the base, splitting it into two right-angled triangles.
scenes.narration: The most common helpful line of all is a height. Dropping a perpendicular splits an awkward triangle into two right-angled ones, which are much easier to work with.

scenes.visual: Lines: "Add a line only with a purpose", "Parallels move angles; heights make right angles", "A grid makes lengths and areas exact".
scenes.narration: Add a line only when you can say why. Parallel lines carry angles; heights create right angles; a grid makes areas exact. Notebook challenge: on a grid, a tilted square has sides that each go two across and one up. What is its area?

notebook_exercise: On a grid, a tilted square has sides going 2 across and 1 up. What is its area?
notebook_answer: Surrounding 3 by 3 square (9) minus four triangles of area 1: 5.
